questions.body: A survey stratifies districts by urbanisation before sampling villages within each stratum. Compared with simple random sampling of the same size, what is the expected effect on the variance of a state-level estimate?

options.label: Variance falls, because within-stratum variation is smaller than overall variation
Variance rises, because stratification adds a second stage of selection
Variance is unchanged, since the total sample size is the same
Variance becomes impossible to estimate without a design effect correction

solutions.value: Stratification groups similar units together. Because variation inside each stratum is smaller than variation across the whole population, the estimate is more precise for the same sample size.

questions.body: An item's price rises from ₹40 to ₹50 and it carries a weight of 6 per cent in the group. What is its contribution to the group index, taking the base as 100?

options.label: 7.5 points
1.5 points
10.0 points
6.0 points

solutions.value: The price relative is 50/40 × 100 = 125. Weighted contribution is 125 × 0.06 = 7.5 index points.

questions.body: A consumption survey asks households to recall spending on food over the past 30 days and on clothing over the past 365 days. What is the main reason for using different reference periods?

options.label: Frequently purchased items are recalled accurately only over short periods
Longer reference periods reduce the total number of households needed
Clothing prices change more slowly than food prices
Statistical software requires uniform annualised inputs

solutions.value: Recall accuracy falls as the period lengthens, but rare purchases need a long window to be captured at all. Reference periods are matched to purchase frequency.

questions.body: Of 8,000 sampled households, 6,800 responded. What is the non-response rate, and why does it matter beyond sample size?

options.label: 15 per cent — non-respondents may differ systematically from respondents
15 per cent — it only reduces precision, introducing no bias
85 per cent — it measures the achieved sample
12 per cent — it is calculated against the responding total

solutions.value: 1,200 of 8,000 is 15 per cent. The real risk is bias: if those who did not respond differ from those who did, weighting the achieved sample up will not fix it.

questions.body: A survey dataset has one row per household with twelve monthly expenditure columns. Which pandas operation converts it to one row per household-month?

options.label: df.melt() to move columns into rows
df.pivot() to spread rows into columns
df.groupby() to aggregate by household
df.merge() to join on the household identifier

solutions.value: melt reshapes wide to long, turning the twelve month columns into a month column and a value column.

questions.body: You need each district's total expenditure alongside every individual household row, without collapsing the rows. What handles this in one query?

options.label: A window function such as SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY district)
GROUP BY district with SUM(expenditure)
A LEFT JOIN of the table onto itself
SELECT DISTINCT district with an ORDER BY

solutions.value: A window function computes an aggregate across a partition while keeping every original row. GROUP BY would collapse them to one row per district.

questions.body: A model flagging suspect survey records has precision 0.95 and recall 0.40. What does this mean in practice?

options.label: Flags are usually correct, but most bad records go undetected
Most bad records are caught, but many flags are false alarms
The model performs well on both measures
The model is overfitted to the training data

solutions.value: High precision means the flags it raises are trustworthy. Low recall means it is missing 60 per cent of the records it should have caught.

questions.body: Before releasing household microdata, which action best reduces the risk of identifying an individual respondent?

options.label: Suppress or collapse cells where very few households share a rare combination of attributes
Remove the name field and publish everything else unchanged
Publish only to registered researchers with no changes to the data
Round every monetary value to the nearest rupee

solutions.value: Names are not the risk. A rare combination of age, occupation, location and household size can identify someone on its own, so small cells are suppressed or collapsed.

questions.body: A senior official asks that an unfavourable release be delayed until after an unrelated announcement. Which principle of official statistics speaks most directly to this?

options.label: Statistics must be released on a pre-announced, impartial schedule
Statistical agencies should consult stakeholders before publishing
Confidentiality of individual respondents must be protected
Agencies should use the most cost-effective collection methods

solutions.value: Impartiality and a pre-announced release calendar protect statistics from being timed for political convenience. That is the safeguard being tested here.

questions.body: An estimate is 6.2 per cent with a 95 per cent confidence interval of 5.8 to 6.6. How should this be conveyed in a press note?

options.label: Report 6.2 per cent and state the range within which the true value very likely falls
Report 6.2 per cent alone, since the interval will confuse readers
Report the range only, since a single figure implies false precision
Report 6.2 per cent and note the result is not statistically significant

solutions.value: Readers need the headline figure to be usable and the interval to understand its precision. Dropping either misleads, and significance is a different claim entirely.
